title: Winery Management & Entrepreneurship
description: The full picture of running a Burgundy winery: business models, financial planning, brand building, sustainability, HR management, and risk management

lessons.0.slides.0.title: Winery Business Model Analysis
lessons.0.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 1 - 17 min
lessons.0.slides.1.title: Domaine vs Négociant Models
lessons.0.slides.2.title: Emerging Trend: The Hybrid Domaine–Négociant Model
lessons.0.slides.2.content: Many modern Burgundy producers use a hybrid model: core products from their own vineyards (Domaine), while also purchasing grapes or wine (Négociant) to expand the product range. Domaine Faiveley, for example, is both a top domaine and a large négociant. This model balances quality control with commercial flexibility.

lessons.1.title: Winery Financial Planning
lessons.1.slides.0.title: Winery Financial Planning
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 2 - 18 min
lessons.1.slides.1.title: 💰 Initial Investment Costs
lessons.1.slides.1.points.0: Land purchase — Burgundy Grand Cru: €1–3 million/hectare
lessons.1.slides.1.points.1: Vineyard establishment — planting, trellising, irrigation systems
lessons.1.slides.1.points.2: Cellar equipment — stainless-steel tanks, oak barrels, bottling line
lessons.1.slides.1.points.3: Buildings — winery, storage cellar, tasting room
lessons.1.slides.1.points.4: Working capital — at least 3 years of operating expenses
lessons.1.slides.1.points.5: Total investment — a small boutique winery requires at least €2 million
lessons.1.slides.2.title: 💰 Winery Start-Up Cost Breakdown (Small Boutique Winery — Total €2 million)
lessons.1.slides.2.content: Land purchase accounts for 50% and is the biggest cost. Grand Cru land at €1–3 million/ha — a small winery needs at least €2 million total. Cash flow is the biggest challenge: 4–5 years with no income.
lessons.1.slides.3.title: Micro-Boutique Winery Start-Up Capital Structure
lessons.1.slides.4.title: The Cash-Flow Challenge
lessons.1.slides.4.content: The biggest challenge in running a winery is cash flow: no income in the first year of planting; the first grapes come in year three; after vinification the wine needs 1–2 years of ageing before bottling; after bottling 6 more months before sale. This means at least 4–5 years with no income but continuing outgoings (labour, equipment, maintenance). Substantial capital or external financing is therefore essential.
lessons.1.slides.5.title: ⏳ Winery Cash-Flow Timeline: The 4–5 Year Journey from Planting to First Income
lessons.1.slides.5.content: A new winery takes at least 4–5 years to generate first income, with ongoing outgoings exceeding €1 million in the interim. After the year-3 harvest there is still 1–2 years of ageing. Cash flow is the single greatest challenge in starting a winery!

lessons.2.title: Brand Building and Marketing
lessons.2.slides.0.title: Brand Building and Marketing
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 3 - 16 min
lessons.2.slides.1.title: 🌟 Brand-Building Strategies
lessons.2.slides.1.points.0: Quality first — the foundation of everything
lessons.2.slides.1.points.3: Media exposure — critic scores, press coverage
lessons.2.slides.1.points.4: Word-of-mouth marketing — sommelier and merchant recommendations
lessons.2.slides.1.points.6: Tasting-room experience — domaine visits, tasting events
lessons.2.slides.2.title: The Importance of Critics
lessons.2.slides.2.content: In Burgundy, critic scores have an enormous impact on sales. The ratings of specialists such as Allen Meadows (Burghound), Jasper Morris MW, and Neal Martin can determine a wine's market price and demand. 90+ is the entry ticket; 95+ can double the price. However, over-reliance on scores carries risks — building one's own brand recognition is essential.

lessons.3.title: Sustainable Management and Organic Certification
lessons.3.slides.0.title: Sustainable Management and Organic Certification
lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 4 - 15 min
lessons.3.slides.1.title: 🌱 Certification Types
lessons.3.slides.1.points.0: Organic (Agriculture Biologique) — no synthetic pesticides or fertilisers
lessons.3.slides.1.points.2: HVE (Haute Valeur Environnementale) — French government certification
lessons.3.slides.1.points.5: B Corp — corporate social responsibility certification
lessons.3.slides.2.title: The Business Value of Sustainability
lessons.3.slides.2.content: Sustainability is not just an ideology — it is a business strategy: (1) younger consumers prefer environmentally conscious products; (2) organic/biodynamic certification can raise prices 15–30%; (3) long-term soil health ensures quality; (4) positive media and market image; (5) attracting investors and partners. DRC, Leroy, and other top domaines all practise biodynamics.
lessons.3.slides.3.title: 🌱 Market Price Premium for Different Certification Types (vs Conventional Farming)
lessons.3.slides.3.content: Biodynamic certification commands the highest premium (25–30%); organic the next (15–20%). Consumers are willing to pay for environmental values, but certification takes time and money.

lessons.4.title: Human Resources Management
lessons.4.slides.0.title: Human Resources Management
lessons.4.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 5 - 16 min
lessons.4.slides.1.title: 👥 Key Winery Positions
lessons.4.slides.1.points.0: Winemaker — the technical core, determines quality
lessons.4.slides.1.points.1: Vineyard manager — specialist in growing and viticulture management
lessons.4.slides.1.points.3: Sales manager — market development and client relationships
lessons.4.slides.1.points.6: Seasonal workers — temporary labour during harvest
lessons.4.slides.2.title: Talent Challenges
lessons.4.slides.2.content: Burgundy faces a labour shortage: young people are reluctant to take on physically demanding vineyard work; qualified winemakers are scarce and expensive; seasonal workers are hard to find (harvest lasts only 2–3 weeks). Solutions include: raising salaries and benefits, providing training opportunities, mechanisation to reduce labour requirements, international recruitment, and cultivating succession through family.

lessons.5.title: Risk Management and Insurance
lessons.5.slides.0.title: Risk Management and Insurance
lessons.5.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 6 - 14 min
lessons.5.slides.1.title: ⚠️ Major Risks
lessons.5.slides.1.points.0: Climate risk — spring frost, hail, drought, heavy rain
lessons.5.slides.1.points.1: Pests and disease — downy mildew, powdery mildew, grape moth
lessons.5.slides.1.points.2: Market risk — falling demand, price volatility
lessons.5.slides.1.points.4: Legal risk — labour law, environmental regulations, tax
lessons.5.slides.1.points.5: Reputational risk — quality issues, negative press
lessons.5.slides.2.title: The Impact of Climate Change
lessons.5.slides.2.content: Climate change is Burgundy's greatest long-term threat: earlier harvests (2–3 weeks earlier over the past 30 years), rising alcohol, falling acidity, and more extreme weather. Spring frosts in 2021 cut production by 50%. Coping strategies: diversify regions, adapt growing techniques, take out climate insurance, and build emergency reserves.
lessons.5.slides.3.title: ⚠️ Burgundy Climate Disasters — Historical Yield Losses (Increasing Frequency of Extreme Events)
lessons.5.slides.3.content: The frequency of extreme weather events has increased over the past 20 years. The 2021 spring frost was record-breaking (–50%); the 2022 drought caused –25%. A major disaster occurs every 3–5 years — wineries must incorporate climate risk into their financial planning.
